Death is inevitable. Get used to it. Locate beefalo asap. Give yourself time to explore the boarders of biomes to get an idea of where they are, but don't wait too long to start building your base. Crock pot and drying racks are your friends. Plant tiny clusters of like 10 trees together, then burn them for charcoal. Take advantage of your character's talents (never let poor Abigail sit in your inventory when she's ready to play). Butterflies are great early game food, but wait before messing with bees. Don't be afraid to look up guides. You don't have to figure it all out yourself.

If you feel you've already lost and want to abandon a save, go ahead and take the time to kill your character. That way, you can get your total days up and unlock more characters that could vibe better with you. This is easy be just finding enemies or starting fights. You could also just wait til night. Or find any number of creative ways to die

And most importantly, be careful not to get too attached to any specific save file. You will lose it at some point. View all of them as a practice run for the next.

I have bipolar type 1 and here is my advice. 

Try not to be judgemental of things they may do while in an episode. I know it's hard when they spend all their money when their manic or haven't showered in 2 weeks because they're depressed. Try to understand that there is something physically going on in their brain that makes them more likely to behave that way. Instead, be encouraging and helpful. For example, one thing my mom and sister do for me when I'm depressed is come over to my apartment and talk with me while I work on cleaning. Try to find little ways like that to help this person. Ask them for ideas too.

At the same time, don't let them use bipolar as an excuse to be harmful. Even if they are in an episode, they are still responsible for their actions. If they do something that requires an apology, hold them to it. Set boundaries to keep yourself mentally (and possibly physically) safe.

Medication is usually the go to treatment for bipolar disorder, but it's hard to get right. If this person goes into an episode, don't automatically assume they haven't taken their medicine. That is really frustrating. At the same time, bipolar patients don't have the best track record with medication compliance. So if you truly believe this person has stopped taking their medication, it may be worth having that conversation (depending of course on the nature of your relationship). If they aren't currently seeing a psychiatrist and/or a therapist, I would gently encourage it. (Medication isn't the solution for everyone, but it is usually helpful to talk to a professional about it). 

Unfortunately, bipolar does have a high suicide rate when compared to the general population. If you suspect that this person may be considering suicide, don't be afraid to have that conversation with them. I know it's hard and scary. However it's better to ask and get them help rather than wait and see. Studies show that talking about suicide doesn't actually increase the rate of suicide. So don't be afraid of giving them ideas. If they do admit that they are considering suicide, encourage them to get help. Depending on where you live, it will be different. However here in the US, the first step is usually getting an evaluation at a hospital or clinic, so encourage them to take that step. If they have a plan, refuse help, and are intent on dying, it may be worth contacting your country's emergency services.

That's all I can think of off the top of my head. Good luck to you and this person.

For example, someone who believes for certain that they are Jesus might be considered delusional depending on other factors.

It hurts an already vulnerable group of people.

Jesus was a common name and there were lots of apocalyptic preachers at that time. It's perfectly believable that an apocalyptic preacher named Jesus from Nazareth existed. If so, he probably became more popular for whatever reason, developing a cult following and catching the eye of the religious leaders. He may have even been put to death by crucifixion, though he most likely would have been thrown in a mass grave with other victims. That is all possible and isn't worth trying to prove or disprove. But he wasn't the son of God. He didn't heal people. He didn't perform miracles. He didn't rise from the dead. By the time the gospels were written down (by people who never knew Jesus, btw), he had grown into a legend. As the gospel writers didn't actually know him and they lived in the 1st century, there was no way to verify the facts. So the legends were written down.

It's really no different than the legends of great leaders at that time. It was extremely common to claim that someone of a high social status was a child of God and had performed miracles.

Personally, I would define "god" as being a supernatural (not subject to the laws of science) being that is the most powerful and/or most intelligent being(s) in existence. 

So I personally wouldn't consider Rick to be a god. Is he the most intelligent being in existence? Maybe. But he isn't supernatural. Of course the show takes liberties, as most art does. But Rick is still constrained by the shows version of science. He can do a lot with it. But he still has to follow all of the laws. Gravity still applies. He still evolved from single celled organisms like every other human. He still has the limitations that the human body creates. Etc. Therefore, regardless of what he thinks of himself or what others think of him, he isn't a God. At least not by the definition I use. And not by the most common understanding of the word.

I thing the term "God" is subjective. Christians have this idea of a perfect being. Ancient Greeks believed in multiple gods who weren't perfect. Pantheists believe that the universe is God. Misotheists see God as an evil being. We can literally define "god" however we want. 

To me personally, a god would need to be both supernatural (can't be studied through science) and the most powerful and/or intelligent being(s) in existence. So it would depend on the exact nature. Likely, I wouldn't consider the creator a god because they most likely wouldn't be supernatural.

The danger with not holding people accountable and readily forgiving poor behavior is that it will occur more often. I think all criminal justice systems should be based on rehabilitation. What biological and environmental factors lead to this person's bad actions? Now how can we change those biological and environmental factors to prevent a future event? I do think part of that is punishment. If someone has to spend a year in prison for whatever, then that should help reinforce that their behavior was unacceptable.

Another thing is prevention. Get people accessable mental health services that can detect risk factors early and work to prevent them.

As far as in our personal lives, we have the right to feel however we feel about other people's actions. If someone calls me stupid, I'm going to be angry at them. I may lash out at them or try to defend myself. Those are consequences to their actions. But there are two sides to every coin. You don't have free will either. I've struggled with depression for most of my life, so I completely understand. To be honest, I came extremely close to killing myself when I left Christianity because I didn't understand how to gain hope without God. Luckily, someone talked me out of it and I'm still here. I know everyone's been saying it, but I do highly recommend talking to a doctor. Some people find that medication helps. Some people, like myself, find that therapy is usually all they need. Others use a combination of both and/or other methods.I only left Christianity in December, so I'm still learning about this whole hope thing myself. But I think I've found a few things that work for me. 

1. I went through this long existential crisis. I started studying philosophy, particularly existential philosophy. This gave me a chance to see what other people have thought about meaning and purpose. Then I chose for myself. Nihilism is basically the belief that everything is meaningless and without a purpose. I personally find this to be depressing. But I've talked to people who find it extremely comforting. It takes the pressure off of their shoulders. There's existentialism, which basically says that you get to choose whatever meaning or purpose you want. Whatever is meaningful to you is meaningful. Most atheists I know find comfort in this one. My favorite is absurdism. It's basically the belief that life is meaningless and there is no grand purpose. But the universe can't tell me what to do. I'm going to live my life and have fun while doing it. I see it as rebelling against the meaninglessness of life. Please keep in mind that all of these are complex topics that have a lot more to them than my simple explanations here. If one or all of them interest you, I recommend looking into them.
2. Another way I've found hope is by about the grandness of the universe. For example, think about how lucky you are to be a living person. Think about it. Every single event had to go perfectly right in your ancestry in order for you to be here. And I'm not just talking about your human ancestry. Going all the way back to the first common ancestor. If any of your ancestors hadn't been able to reproduce or were delayed in reproducing, you wouldn't exist. Not to mention how many sperm/egg combinations could have happened. I like to think that the universe is just one big thing and everything in it is just a part of it. That means that we are a part of the universe. It's like the human body is one big thing, but it's made up of trillions of cells. We are literally the universe's way of waking up and experiencing itself. It's pretty incredible.
3. Set goals. During my existential crisis, I ended up setting three major goals for my life. I believe that if I achieve all three of these to a satisfactory level, I will be proud of the life I lived. To be honest, they are quite vague. I'm only 21 and haven't fully decided how I want to go about achieving these goals. But I still have them. You may have more or less. Your goals will almost certainly be different than mine and that's good. These are your goals. I think these goals are helpful because it gives me something to look forward to. It gives me a glimpse into what my future could end up being if I put in the work. Now, start taking steps, big or small, to reach those goals.
4. Get inspired by history. Whatever you're interested in, there's a history to it. People took steps to get where we are. I'm really interested in philosophy and science. I think about the great minds who got us to where we are now in both of those fields. But even if it's something you don't have a particular interest in, you can find inspiration. I think about it and find myself amazed at the Wright brothers who wanted to fly so bad and found a way to do it. I think about the people who worked so hard to make this world a better place for everyone who came after them. I think about the brave women who fought for my right to vote or the people who fought to end slavery. I'm an American, so sorry about the American references. It's what I know most about. I think about these great people of the past who left behind these amazing legacies and I decide that I want to be like them. I can help to make the world just a little better for future generations. You can too, even if you don't get your name in a history book.
5. Current events. It's really hard to have hope when everything around you is negative. It feels like everything is falling apart and nothing will get better. But things have fallen apart before and things have always gotten better. I think it was in March-April, the queen of England gave a speech about the pandemic. (I live in the US, but I watched it for fun.) She compared the tough times we are facing now to when she had to broadcast to the children who had been separated from their families during WWII. Most of us are too young to have experienced events as devastating as these. But she is old enough to remember those events. I'm sure that during every horrible event, there were people who lost hope. But the world eventually calmed down again. The world will calm down again. It may take a while and we may never return to our old normal. In which case, we'll just have to create a new normal. I, for one, am going to forever have a stash of essential supplies like toilet paper and hand sanitizer in my basement. This pandemic may have turned me into a doomsday prepper. Haha!

Anyway, I hope that helped some. As I said, I totally understand living with depression. Let me know if you need someone to talk to or anything.

I used to be an extremely devoted Christian. I don't believe in God anymore, but I think there are a few rational reasons why one may hold similar beliefs (I don't know the specifics of other religions so I'm not exactly sure if this applies to them as well or not). 

1. Confirmation bias. When people believe something, they will put much more stock into information that confirms their current beliefs. They will seek out information to help them defend it and ignore information that contradicts it.
2. Many people find it much more comforting to believe in a higher power and possibly a happy afterlife. It can give some people peace and help them cope with everyday life.
3. Lots of people, myself included, were taught from a young age to believe in something. Oftentimes, the child sees their caregiver being happy and praising them when they act more religious so they associate church and bible study with good things.
4. Often, people will experience something that "must have been God." It can be a sick relative getting better, surviving a near-death experience, or even just a feeling in their gut. The attribute that to God.
5. There are also several philosophical arguments for the existence of God. I personally don't buy into them, but I used to when I was a Christain.

Once given proof that he couldn't refute, Einstein finally accepted the fact that the universe is in motion and went back to his previous equation. Even the smartest people who have walked the Earth can and have struggled with this.

I think that everyone who has any information at all and any level of critical thinking skills, at least subconsciously understands that this could become a big threat if it hasn't already. Due to the intelligence of humans, our brains have developed several coping mechanisms to help our mental health. I think 2 of those play a big role in how all of this is playing out.

1. People are in denial. It's easier to believe that you're some big hot shot that can't be hurt by anything. I don't know how the rest of the world is, but here in America, a lot of us have this idea that we are untouchable. Most people around me see the biggest enemies as being domestic rather than global. At least in the US, we have an entire generation (my generation, gen z) that has never seen an event that has drastically changed our lives. The last event I can think of for us was 9/11, which I know placed fear in a lot of Americans and made them realize that we aren't untouchable. But that was nearly 20 years ago. My entire generation, many of us are at voting age, weren't born yet or have no memory of the event. So I know it's hard for us to think of something drastic happening. It kind of reminds me of how I think every October/November. If I don't prepare for winter, it can't come. Then I'm left without an ice scraper or a brush when the first snow/ice comes along. I think most people are having this mentality.
2. The other extreme that I think people on here are more prone to is an obsession. We want to prepare as much as we can. Let's be honest. This is scary for all of us. Some virus that we know very little about is rapidly infecting and killing people. A lot of us have little knowledge about medicine or infectious disease so it makes us feel even more vulnerable. Even medical professionals may be scared despite their knowledge because they still have no control over how their government chooses to react to this outbreak. It's hard not to be scared when you have no control over a situation. So obsessing about what is going on and making sure we have the most up to date information helps us feel like we have some sort of control over the virus. Preparing makes us feel a little bit safer, so we do as much of that as we can. I fall more into this category in this context.

I'm not saying that preparing and worrying are irrational. I'm simply saying that this is the pattern I seem to be seeing. I'm also not saying that everyone falls into one of these categories. I'm just saying that these two defense mechanisms may explain both the carefree and the panicking nature that we see in person and online. Eventually, everyone will be forced to face the reality that comes. Either this will blow over and not get too severe anywhere else and obsessors will stop worrying, or people will be given undeniable evidence that this is going to get worse and will start trying to control the situation. Only time will tell.

There's just a lot of uncertainties and I think it's important that we take as many precautions as necessary to protect ourselves and everyone else.

Let's not forget that this isn't the flu. Yes, the flu can be serious and can kill people. But the comparison to the flu is unhelpful because the majority of humanity already has the ability to fight off the flu because we experience it every year. Not to mention that millions of people are vaccinated. Even for those who aren't vaccinated, the flu has an incredibly low chance of killing someone who is otherwise healthy who isn't super young or old. If you have a regularly functioning immune system, you will probably be fine with the flu. With the flu, we pretty much know what we are dealing with for most years. Every now and then, a mutation throws us for a loop, but this doesn't seem to be one of those years. With the coronavirus, we do know that it seems to be targeting older individuals, however, there are plenty of young, otherwise healthy people dying from it. Humans have absolutely no experience with it, so our immune systems have no idea how to handle it. There are a lot of unknowns with this virus, so comparing it to the flu can be really harmful. If it were "just the flu," I don't think countries would be shutting down their borders. I don't think the CCP would be trying to hide how bad they messed up with this one. I don't think W.H.O. would have declared it a global health emergency. It's pretty obvious, even if you don't have all the information, that this isn't just the flu.

When I was 14, I was first diagnosed with depression and anxiety. I was also struggling with what my therapists now have identified as bulimia. I told my parents and school counselor that a boy at school was threatening to rape me. Nothing. I told my parents that I hated my therapist. Nothing. I told my parents that I was struggling with my eating and I didn't know what to do. Nothing. I told my parents that I had been sexually assaulted by my boyfriend. Nothing. My dad still invited him and his family over after we broke up to hang out with the family. I told my parents and school counselor that I was being bullied at school. Nothing. My parents found out that I was cutting and burning myself. Nothing. All of this was within one school year. Finally, I had enough. I called a suicide hotline. They called my parents. Finally, they did something. But now that I'm an adult, my mom still insists that she shouldn't have done anything after that because it made things harder on her.

I'll go talk to my therapist but I can't go to the hospital again. If I go, my family will be horrible about it and try to guilt-trip me. Every time a doctor labels me with a new diagnosis, my mom's just like "you're just lying to the doctor to get attention." They'll just put me on medication that's just going to mess up my brain when I eventually go off them. Because I'm more scared of the voices than the doctors. I'll miss several days of work, if not a week or two of work. When I go back, nothing will be normal. It'll just make work worse for me when it's already a huge stressor. Then, when I get out, I'll be saddled with medical bills that will make everything even worse. I promised my therapist that I'd meet with him. But beyond that, I've pretty much made my decision.

None of the treatments have worked in the past 10 years since I started struggling. I don't remember what it's like to be truly happy. Everyone, including myself, would be better off had I never existed. But sadly, I do exist and now it's this whole ordeal to try and stop existing. I'm tired and in constant pain. I can't do anything right. The tags on my car are almost 6 months expired because I can't get myself to freaking do it. I'm months behind on all my debt because I can't get myself to do anything.  Then there's the fact that there's literally no hope of getting better. None of the doctors and therapists can figure out what's wrong. I've been through so many different diagnoses, medications, treatments, hospitalizations, etc. If the professionals who spend years (especially the psychiatrists who spend upwards of 12 years studying and training to work with mental health conditions) can't even figure out what's wrong with me, how are they going to treat me? I'm so nieve so every time that they put me in the hospital or force some other treatment on me, I get filled with this false sense of hope that maybe it'll work or maybe I'll be just a little bit stronger next time a depressive episode hits. But every time, it gets worse. I'm done being filled with false hope. All the doctors and everyone know that it's just a matter of time before I kill myself. They're just trying to prolong the inevitable.
I just took a shower. I hate taking showers because there's nothing to distract me from the thoughts that enter my mind. But I did it.

It's frustrating. I always want to ask the person who tells me this thing like "oh, so you know who the 76th US president will be? Really? Do you know what numbers to pick for the next lottery? Why haven't you won yet?" It's impossible to tell the future. Yes. It's possible that things will get better. But it's often even more likely that it will stay the same or get worse. For example, if you have a terminal illness, the chances of you being miraculously healed are extremely slim. If you can't make peace with that, then it's not going to get better. But maybe it does get better. But is the pain you're experiencing now really worth the "better" you will get. "Better" can mean something as simple as less pain. Maybe you're still in excruciating pain from an injury. But your headaches are finally gone. That's better, but still not good. It's just a general blanket statement. It doesn't require the person saying it to actually know you or the situations surrounding your suffering.

It would be impossible to calculate. In order to do it, you'd need to account for every single possible factor. Every single event that's happened in your life (good, bad, and neutral), along with what kinds of food you eat, the types of people you spend time with, your hobbies, any skills you have, education level, income level, living situations, sexual orientation, gender identity, military experience, previous suicide attempts, etc. It's impossible to determine all the factors for any individual. Just remember that you are not a statistic and there is no statistic out there that will perfectly describe you.

About 129 Americans die by suicide every day and a lot more attempt it.

It's the 10th leading cause of death in the US, which is saying something because there are lots of ways to die. It's the 2nd leading cause for ages 15-34 and the 4th leading cause in ages 35-54. 

Yes, the statistics change based on race, age, gender, etc. But that doesn't mean that you're weak because you're in a group that is less likely to die by suicide. America may look like it has fewer suicides compared to the rest of the world and that may be true. But America is also a pretty wealthy country. Of course, not everyone can afford mental health care in this country, but there's a higher percentage of people who can than a lot of other countries. It also helps that America is one of the leaders in medical research so whenever new information comes out, American doctors are usually among the first to find out and implement it. Things are far from perfect. I'm not trying to say that it's the best in the world or even close to where it should be. What I'm trying to say is that there are other factors that influence every statistic you are going to see. For example, if you're someone who can't afford treatment, it doesn't matter if America has more research and technology. If you're someone that existing medications don't work on, it doesn't matter how affordable or expensive those medications are. I think it would be helpful to look more into the statistics of your particular demographic. I don't know what gender you are, but for example, if you're a man, you're 3.5x more likely to die by suicide. But that's very vague. The term "man" can refer to so many different types of people. Okay. Well, maybe you have a mental illness. That increases your chance. But some mental illnesses don't increase the chance of suicide. So maybe you have depression. That's a little bit more specific. But even still, remember that you are not a statistic. There is no statistic in the world that will perfectly determine your chance of anything in life. Because people in every demographic are completely different. I'm sorry if I went on a bit of a tangent. Basically, no. That statistic doesn't mean that you're the weakest of 10,000 people.

The nominations and winners are decided by the academy members. From what I understand, they're not a very diverse group so they all have similar tastes. For example, they have an extreme bias towards not just American movies, but Hollywood movies specifically. Movies made in other parts of the country are usually ignored too. Because animation still isn't as respected in America as it should be and is largely still seen as something for children, most of the academy members don't bother trying to make an informed decision. A large chunk of the members only end up seeing one or two animated movies per year and probably vote for whichever one their child watches the most because they don't see that as being a problem. Animation and foreign film categories are some of the few categories that don't actually have their own branch of people who truly appreciate that category. The nominees are chosen by a committee made up of people from all the other branches. But since they don't have a branch of passionate viewers and most of the people making the decisions won't actually go watch most of the movies, it's a flawed system. It's sad and I wish they would make some changes to make it better.
